title: Primitives in JavaScript
idea: A primitive is a single, immutable value: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null or symbol. Variables hold it directly, and `===` compares it by value.

analogy.text: A number written on a sticky note. Copying it onto a second note gives two independent notes; changing one leaves the other alone.
analogy.breaks: Primitives are never edited; a variable is given a new value.

points: There are seven primitive types; everything else is an object.
Primitives are immutable: `toUpperCase()` returns a new string and leaves the old one.
Assigning a primitive copies it, so changing one variable never affects another.
`===` compares primitives by value, and `typeof` reports the type name.

pitfalls: Check for null with `value === null`; `typeof value === 'object'` also matches arrays and objects.
Never compare decimal results with `===`; use integer cents or a small tolerance.
Test for NaN with `Number.isNaN(x)`; `x === NaN` is always false.

quiz.why: `y` is a copy, so `x` stays 5. `typeof null` is the string "object".

takeaway: Primitives are copied and compared by value, and never change in place.
